{{Short description|Review of astronomy literature produced every ten years}}
[[File:The Galactic Centre and Bulge above the ESO 3.6-metre telescope.jpg|thumb|right|250px|The [[Milky Way]] as viewed from [[La Silla Observatory]]]]
The '''Astronomy and Astrophysics Decadal Survey''' is a review of [[astronomy]] and [[astrophysics]] literature produced approximately every ten years by the [[United States National Research Council|National Research Council]] of the [[United States National Academy of Sciences|National Academy of Sciences]] in the United States. The report surveys the current state of the field, identifies research priorities, and makes recommendations for the coming decade. The [[decadal survey]] represents the recommendations of the research community to governmental agencies on how to prioritize scientific funding within astronomy and astrophysics. The editing committee is informed by topical panels and subcommittees, dedicated [[Academic conference|conferences]], and direct community input in the form of [[white paper]]s summarizing the state of the art in each subdiscipline. The most recent report, Astro2020, was released in 2021.<ref name="NA-20211104" /><ref name="Astro2010_input">{{cite web |website=The National Academies of Sciences, Engineering, and Medicine |url=http://sites.nationalacademies.org/BPA/BPA_049526 |title=Astro2010: The Astronomy and Astrophysics Decadal Survey — Community Input to the Survey |access-date=2010-09-09 |archive-date=2019-10-26 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20191026110156/http://sites.nationalacademies.org/BPA/BPA_049526 |url-status=dead }}</ref><ref name="Astro2010_estab">{{cite book |url= https://www.nap.edu/catalog/12951/new-worlds-new-horizons-in-astronomy-and-astrophysics |title=New Worlds, New Horizons in Astronomy and Astrophysics |author=National Research Council |date=2010 |location=Washington, DC |publisher=The National Academies Press |doi=10.17226/12951 |isbn=978-0-309-15799-5 |access-date= 2017-12-05}}</ref><ref name="Astro2010_Space.com">{{cite news|title=Anticipation High for New Decadal Astronomy Report |date=2010-08-13 |url=http://www.space.com/news/anticipation-high-astronomy-decadal-report-100813.html |work=[[Space.com]] |access-date=2010-09-09 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20100915112004/http://www.space.com/news/anticipation-high-astronomy-decadal-report-100813.html |archive-date=2010-09-15 |url-status=live }}</ref>

== Ground-Based Astronomy: A Ten-Year Program, 1964 ==
The first report, ''Ground-Based Astronomy: A Ten-Year Program'', was released in 1964.<ref name="Astro1964">{{cite book | last1 = National Academy of Sciences (U.S.). Panel on Astronomical Facilities | title = Ground-based astronomy: a ten-year program | publisher = [[National Academies Press]] | year = 1964 | url = https://books.google.com/books?id=JnErAAAAYAAJ | access-date = 2010-09-09}}</ref> The authoring committee was chaired by [[Albert Whitford (astronomer)|Albert Whitford]]. The report recommends construction of national observing facilities, including especially mid-sized ground-based optical telescopes.<ref name="NRAO_timeline">{{cite web | url = http://www.nrao.edu/archives/Timeline/timeline.shtml | title = National Radio Astronomy Observatory Archives: NRAO Timeline | access-date = 2010-09-09 | archive-date = 2020-07-26 | archive-url = https://web.archive.org/web/20200726103033/https://www.nrao.edu/archives/Timeline/timeline.shtml }}</ref><ref name="3rd_AADS">{{cite book |title=Astronomy and astrophysics for the 1980s |publisher=[[National Academy Press]] |location=Washington, D.C. |year=1982 |isbn=0-309-03249-0 |url-access=registration |url=https://archive.org/details/astronomyastroph0000asse }}</ref>

== Astronomy and Astrophysics for the 1970s, 1972 ==
The second report, ''Astronomy and Astrophysics for the 1970s'', was released in 1972.<ref name="2nd_AADS">{{cite book |title=Astronomy and astrophysics for the 1970s |publisher=National Academy of Sciences |location=Washington |year=1972 |isbn=0-309-02110-3 }}</ref> The committee was chaired by [[Jesse L. Greenstein]]. It recommends priorities for both space- and ground-based programs, and was instrumental in the eventual construction of the [[Very Large Array]].<ref name="NRAO_timeline" /><ref name="3rd_AADS" />

== Astronomy and Astrophysics for the 1980s, 1982 ==
The third report, ''Astronomy and Astrophysics for the 1980s'', was released in 1982.<ref name="3rd_AADS" /> The committee was chaired by [[George B. Field]]. It recommended the launch of the "Advanced X-Ray Astrophysics Facility", which was realized in 1999 as the [[Chandra X-ray Observatory]].<ref name="Weisskopf2010">{{Cite journal|last1=Weisskopf|first1=M. C.|year=2010|title=Chandra's First Decade of Discovery Special Feature: the making of the Chandra X-Ray Observatory: the project scientist's perspective|journal=Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences|volume=107|issue=16|pages=7135–7140|arxiv=1003.1990|bibcode=2010PNAS..107.7135W|doi=10.1073/pnas.0913067107|pmid=20194740|pmc=2867751|doi-access=free}}</ref> It also identified construction of the [[Very Long Baseline Array]] as a priority, in addition to briefly mentioning the [[Hubble Space Telescope]] (before it received that name) and the Shuttle Infrared Telescope Facility (later [[Spitzer Space Telescope|Spitzer]]).<ref name="NRAO_timeline" />

== The Decade of Discovery in Astronomy and Astrophysics, 1991 ==
The fourth report, ''The Decade of Discovery in Astronomy and Astrophysics'', was released in 1991.<ref name="4th_AADS">{{cite book |title=The decade of discovery in astronomy and astrophysics |url=https://archive.org/details/decadeofdiscover0000nati|url-access=registration|publisher=National Academy Press |location=Washington, D.C. |year=1991 |isbn=0-309-04381-6 }}</ref>  The committee was chaired by [[John N. Bahcall]]. It recommended the launch of the "Space Infrared Telescope Facility", realized in 2003 as the [[Spitzer Space Telescope]],<ref name="Astro1991_SST">{{cite web | url = http://www.nasa.gov/mission_pages/spitzer/infrared/recent.html | title = Spitzer Mission Overview | access-date = 2010-09-09| archive-url= https://web.archive.org/web/20100811213623/http://www.nasa.gov/mission_pages/spitzer/infrared/recent.html| archive-date= 11 August 2010 <!--DASHBot-->| url-status=live}}</ref> the fourth and final in NASA's [[Great Observatories program]].

== Astronomy and Astrophysics in the New Millennium, 2001 ==
The fifth report, ''Astronomy and Astrophysics in the New Millennium'', was released in 2001.<ref name="5th_AADS">{{cite book |title=Astronomy and astrophysics in the new millennium |publisher=National Academy Press |location=Washington, D.C. |year=2001 |isbn=0-309-07312-X }}</ref> The committee was co-chaired by [[Christopher McKee]] and [[Joseph Hooton Taylor Jr.|Joseph H. Taylor]]. It gives highest priority to the construction and launch of  Next Generation Space Telescope, now known as the [[James Webb Space Telescope]] which launched on 25 December 2021.<ref>{{Cite web|last=Loff|first=Sarah|url=https://www.nasa.gov/feature/james-webb-space-telescope-launch-update/|title=James Webb Space Telescope Launch Update|date=21 December 2021|access-date=21 December 2021|website=NASA|publisher=NASA}}</ref> The report reaffirms the 1991 recommendation for the completion of the Millimeter Array, now part of the [[Atacama Large Millimeter Array]] international collaboration. It also examines the benefits of a robust astronomy research program to the nation, and expresses concern regarding the percentage of funding tied to a few large projects.<ref name="Astro2001_AIP">{{cite news | first = Richard M. | last = Jones | title = Astronomy and Astrophysics in the New Millennium: NRC sets priorities | date = 2000-06-08 | publisher = [[American Institute of Physics]] | url = http://www.aip.org/fyi/2000/fyi00.062.htm | work = FYI: the AIP bulletin of science policy news | access-date = 2010-09-09 | archive-date = 2020-07-28 | archive-url = https://web.archive.org/web/20200728145112/https://www.aip.org/fyi/2000/fyi00.062.htm | url-status = dead }}</ref>

== New Worlds, New Horizons in Astronomy and Astrophysics, 2010 ==
The sixth report, ''New Worlds, New Horizons in Astronomy and Astrophysics'', was released in 2010.  The committee was chaired by [[Roger D. Blandford]]. Recommendations for scientific questions to be answered include: the nature of [[dark energy]]; the structure, distribution, and evolution of [[Extrasolar planet|exoplanetary systems]]; detailed examination of extreme processes including [[supernovae]] and the merger of superdense objects; and how galaxies and galaxy clusters formed from the early hot universe.<ref name="Astro2010" />{{rp|7}} The report also examines technical readiness, scheduling, and funding issues as well as basic science. The recommendations consider a range of funding scenarios based on projected budgets for the major funding agencies, [[NASA]], the [[National Science Foundation]], and the [[United States Department of Energy|Department of Energy]]. The top priorities identified by the report include:
* Wide-Field Infrared Survey Telescope (WFIRST), now known as the [[Nancy Grace Roman Space Telescope]], a space-based telescope to be located at [[Lagrangian point#L2|Lagrangian point L2]] that will survey and catalogue [[Extrasolar planet|exoplanets]] and may help settle questions of the nature of [[dark energy]].
* [[Large Synoptic Survey Telescope]] (LSST), now known as the [[Vera C. Rubin Observatory]], a wide field ground-based telescope that will provide measurements of [[weak gravitational lensing]] and map and record transient or moving phenomena such as [[supernovae]] and [[near-Earth asteroid]]s.
* [[New Worlds Technology Development Program]] to plan and lay the groundwork for future missions to study nearby Earth-like exoplanets
* [[Cerro Chajnantor Atacama Telescope]] (CCAT), a ground-based telescope sensitive in the millimeter and submillimeter range. CCAT will survey young dusty star systems and galaxies, and serve as a companion to [[Atacama Large Millimeter Array]] at the same site.<ref name="CCAT">{{cite news | title = National Research Council Report Highly Recommends CCAT | date = August 2010 | url = http://www.submm.org/doc/2010-08-ccat-news-11.pdf | work = The CCAT News | access-date = 2010-09-09 | archive-date = 2011-07-28 | archive-url = https://web.archive.org/web/20110728070355/http://www.submm.org/doc/2010-08-ccat-news-11.pdf | url-status = dead }}</ref>

Other priorities include [[Laser Interferometer Space Antenna]] (LISA) for measuring [[gravitational waves]] and [[International X-ray Observatory]] for investigating black holes and the evolution of [[Observable universe#Large-scale structure|large scale structure in the universe]]. The report also recommends augmenting the [[Explorer program]] for small and medium-sized missions with rapid turnaround and high scientific return, and the creation of a Midscale Innovations Program within the [[National Science Foundation]] for funding projects in the $4&ndash;135 million range.<ref name="Astro2010">{{cite book |author=National Research Council  | title = New Worlds, New Horizons in Astronomy and Astrophysics | publisher = [[National Academies Press]] | year = 2010 | url = http://www.nap.edu/catalog.php?record_id=12951 | access-date = 2010-09-09 | isbn = 978-0-309-15796-4| archive-url= https://web.archive.org/web/20100816093222/http://www.nap.edu/catalog.php?record_id=12951| archive-date= 16 August 2010 | url-status=live}}</ref><ref name="Astro2010_PR">{{cite news | title = Report Identifies Top Priorities for Astronomy and Astrophysics in the Coming Decade | date = 2010-08-13 | url = http://www8.nationalacademies.org/onpinews/newsitem.aspx?RecordID=12951 | work = Office of News and Public Relations of the National Academies | access-date = 2010-09-09| archive-url= https://web.archive.org/web/20100817181341/http://www8.nationalacademies.org/onpinews/newsitem.aspx?RecordID=12951| archive-date= 17 August 2010 <!--DASHBot-->| url-status=live}}</ref>

== Pathways to Discovery in Astronomy and Astrophysics for the 2020s ==
The seventh report was published in November 2021 and recommended scientific priorities and investments for the next decade to help achieve the following primary goals: search for [[habitable exoplanet]]s and [[extraterrestrial life]], study [[black hole]]s and [[neutron star]]s and study the [[Galaxy formation and evolution|growth and evolution of galaxies]]. The top priority recommended to the NSF was to combine the [[Thirty Meter Telescope]] and [[Giant Magellan Telescope]] programs into one United States Extremely Large Telescope program. The top priority recommended to NASA was to establish a new Great Observatories Mission and Technology Maturation program that would conduct studies into 2030s-launched telescopes, with a [[Habitable Worlds Observatory|hybrid]] of [[LUVOIR]] (successor to Hubble) and [[HabEx]] (successor to Spitzer) as the first major project with an estimated cost of US$11 billion, to be followed by cheaper [[far-infrared astronomy]] and [[X-ray astronomy]] designs (the [[Origins Space Telescope]] and [[Lynx X-ray Observatory]]) with an estimated cost from US$3 billion to US$5 billion each.<ref>{{cite web |title=Astrophysics decadal survey recommends a program of flagship space telescopes |url=https://spacenews.com/astrophysics-decadal-survey-recommends-a-program-of-flagship-space-telescopes/ |website=SpaceNews |last=Foust |first=Jeff |access-date=4 November 2021 |date=4 November 2021}}</ref><ref name="NYT-20211104">{{cite news |last=Overbye |first=Dennis |author-link=Dennis Overbye |title=A New 10-Year Plan for the Cosmos - On astronomers' wish list for the next decade: two giant telescopes and a space telescope to search for life and habitable worlds beyond Earth. |url=https://www.nytimes.com/2021/11/04/science/astronomy-decadal-survey-telescope.html |date=4 November 2021 |work=[[The New York Times]] |access-date=5 November 2021 }}</ref><ref name="NA-20211104">{{cite news |title=New Report Charts Path for Next Decade of Astronomy and Astrophysics; Recommends Future Ground and Space - Telescopes, Scientific Priorities, Investments in Scientific Community |url=https://www.nationalacademies.org/news/2021/11/new-report-charts-path-for-next-decade-of-astronomy-and-astrophysics-recommends-future-ground-and-space-telescopes-scientific-priorities-investments-in-scientific-community |date=4 November 2021 |work=[[National Academies of Sciences, Engineering, and Medicine]] |access-date=5 November 2021 }}</ref> Additionally, the report recommended the establishment of a new class in the [[Explorers Program]] filling the gap between [[NASA large strategic science missions|flagship missions]] and Medium-Class Explorers.<ref>{{Cite web |title=NASA Establishes New Class of Astrophysics Missions, Selects Studies - NASA |url=https://www.nasa.gov/news-release/nasa-establishes-new-class-of-astrophysics-missions-selects-studies/ |access-date=2026-09-24 |language=en-US}}</ref> NASA formally endorsed and initiated the plans in 2024.<ref name="Foust 2024a">{{cite web | last=Foust | first=Jeff | title=Congressional language alters plans for NASA’s Habitable Worlds Observatory | website=SpaceNews | date=June 4, 2024 | url=https://spacenews.com/congressional-language-alters-plans-for-nasas-habitable-worlds-observatory/ | access-date=December 8, 2024}}</ref><ref name="Foust 2024b">{{cite web | last=Foust | first=Jeff | title=NASA selects X-ray and far-infrared space telescope concepts for study | website=SpaceNews | date=October 4, 2024 | url=https://spacenews.com/nasa-selects-x-ray-and-far-infrared-space-telescope-concepts-for-study/ | access-date=December 8, 2024}}</ref>
